paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the grey wolf was little more than a memory across most of western and central Europe. Centuries of hunting, often encouraged by bounties paid to anyone who produced a dead animal, combined with poisoning and the clearing of forests to push the species out of one country after another. By the 1960s, wolves survived mainly in scattered refuges: the mountains of the Iberian Peninsula, the Apennines of Italy, the Balkans and the great forests of eastern Europe. Today, by contrast, wolves breed in most mainland European countries, and recent estimates put the continent's population at well over ten thousand animals. Few large carnivores anywhere have staged such a comeback, and remarkably, it has happened not in wilderness but in one of the most densely populated and intensively farmed regions on Earth.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first reason for this recovery is legal. For most of history, killing a wolf was not merely permitted but regarded as a public service. That attitude began to change in the 1970s. Italy gave the wolf legal protection in 1971, at a time when perhaps only 100 animals remained in the Apennines. In 1979 the Bern Convention, a European agreement on the conservation of wildlife and natural habitats, listed the wolf as strictly protected, and later European Union law reinforced this status. Some countries, Spain among them, kept exceptions that allowed limited hunting in particular regions, but across much of the continent the threat of being shot was sharply reduced for the first time in centuries.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Changes in the countryside mattered just as much. During the second half of the twentieth century, millions of rural Europeans left the land for jobs in towns and cities. Hillside fields that had been grazed or ploughed for generations were abandoned and slowly returned to scrub and woodland. This process gave wolves both cover and, more importantly, food. Populations of red deer, roe deer and wild boar expanded dramatically, partly because there were fewer people to hunt them and partly because the new forests provided ideal shelter. A predator returning to these landscapes found a far richer supply of wild prey than its ancestors had known a century earlier.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The third factor is the wolf itself. Young wolves usually leave the pack into which they were born at between one and two years old, setting off in search of a mate and a territory of their own. Some travel astonishing distances. Wolves from Italy crossed into the French Alps in the early 1990s, and in 2000 a pair that had wandered west from Poland raised cubs in eastern Germany, the first known breeding there for well over a century. Ilka Brunner, an ecologist who followed forty young wolves fitted with satellite collars, found that some covered more than 800 kilometres before settling and that most crossed roads and farmland mainly at night, when people were indoors. 'They are not creatures of the wilderness,' she says. 'They are adaptable animals that were kept out of our landscapes by guns, not by any lack of suitable habitat.'
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes their return. For sheep and goat farmers, particularly in areas where wolves had been absent for generations, the arrival of a pack can be devastating. In regions where wolves never disappeared, such as central Italy, shepherds kept up traditions of guarding flocks with dogs and bringing animals into enclosures at night. In places like the French Alps or the plains of northern Germany, by contrast, such practices had largely been forgotten, and flocks often grazed unattended for weeks. Aurelio Mancuso, who keeps around 400 sheep in the Abruzzo mountains, believes the real problem is less the wolf than the loss of old skills. 'My grandfather never left his sheep alone,' he says. 'Farmers elsewhere are now having to relearn what we never forgot.' Many governments pay compensation for animals that are killed, but farmers frequently complain that payments arrive late and fail to cover the stress, the extra work or the loss of valuable breeding stock.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Increasingly, therefore, governments are investing in prevention rather than payment. Electric fencing and specially bred guardian dogs, often from traditional breeds such as Italy's Maremma sheepdog, are now subsidised in several countries. Their effectiveness, however, depends heavily on how they are used. Ngozi Abara, a social scientist who interviewed more than 200 livestock owners, found that farmers who received training as well as equipment reported far fewer losses than those who were simply handed fences. She also discovered that attitudes towards wolves were shaped less by the number of animals a farmer had lost than by a sense that decisions were being taken by distant officials. Pressure from rural communities has already led to moves to lower the wolf's protected status and permit more culling. Whether Europe can share its crowded landscapes with a large predator may ultimately depend less on biology than on whether the people who bear the costs feel they are being heard.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
The Return of the Wolf

A. For much of the twentieth century, the grey wolf was little more than a memory across most of western and central Europe. Centuries of hunting, often encouraged by bounties paid to anyone who produced a dead animal, combined with poisoning and the clearing of forests to push the species out of one country after another. By the 1960s, wolves survived mainly in scattered refuges: the mountains of the Iberian Peninsula, the Apennines of Italy, the Balkans and the great forests of eastern Europe. Today, by contrast, wolves breed in most mainland European countries, and recent estimates put the continent's population at well over ten thousand animals. Few large carnivores anywhere have staged such a comeback, and remarkably, it has happened not in wilderness but in one of the most densely populated and intensively farmed regions on Earth.

B. The first reason for this recovery is legal. For most of history, killing a wolf was not merely permitted but regarded as a public service. That attitude began to change in the 1970s. Italy gave the wolf legal protection in 1971, at a time when perhaps only 100 animals remained in the Apennines. In 1979 the Bern Convention, a European agreement on the conservation of wildlife and natural habitats, listed the wolf as strictly protected, and later European Union law reinforced this status. Some countries, Spain among them, kept exceptions that allowed limited hunting in particular regions, but across much of the continent the threat of being shot was sharply reduced for the first time in centuries.

C. Changes in the countryside mattered just as much. During the second half of the twentieth century, millions of rural Europeans left the land for jobs in towns and cities. Hillside fields that had been grazed or ploughed for generations were abandoned and slowly returned to scrub and woodland. This process gave wolves both cover and, more importantly, food. Populations of red deer, roe deer and wild boar expanded dramatically, partly because there were fewer people to hunt them and partly because the new forests provided ideal shelter. A predator returning to these landscapes found a far richer supply of wild prey than its ancestors had known a century earlier.

D. The third factor is the wolf itself. Young wolves usually leave the pack into which they were born at between one and two years old, setting off in search of a mate and a territory of their own. Some travel astonishing distances. Wolves from Italy crossed into the French Alps in the early 1990s, and in 2000 a pair that had wandered west from Poland raised cubs in eastern Germany, the first known breeding there for well over a century. Ilka Brunner, an ecologist who followed forty young wolves fitted with satellite collars, found that some covered more than 800 kilometres before settling and that most crossed roads and farmland mainly at night, when people were indoors. 'They are not creatures of the wilderness,' she says. 'They are adaptable animals that were kept out of our landscapes by guns, not by any lack of suitable habitat.'

E. Not everyone welcomes their return. For sheep and goat farmers, particularly in areas where wolves had been absent for generations, the arrival of a pack can be devastating. In regions where wolves never disappeared, such as central Italy, shepherds kept up traditions of guarding flocks with dogs and bringing animals into enclosures at night. In places like the French Alps or the plains of northern Germany, by contrast, such practices had largely been forgotten, and flocks often grazed unattended for weeks. Aurelio Mancuso, who keeps around 400 sheep in the Abruzzo mountains, believes the real problem is less the wolf than the loss of old skills. 'My grandfather never left his sheep alone,' he says. 'Farmers elsewhere are now having to relearn what we never forgot.' Many governments pay compensation for animals that are killed, but farmers frequently complain that payments arrive late and fail to cover the stress, the extra work or the loss of valuable breeding stock.

F. Increasingly, therefore, governments are investing in prevention rather than payment. Electric fencing and specially bred guardian dogs, often from traditional breeds such as Italy's Maremma sheepdog, are now subsidised in several countries. Their effectiveness, however, depends heavily on how they are used. Ngozi Abara, a social scientist who interviewed more than 200 livestock owners, found that farmers who received training as well as equipment reported far fewer losses than those who were simply handed fences. She also discovered that attitudes towards wolves were shaped less by the number of animals a farmer had lost than by a sense that decisions were being taken by distant officials. Pressure from rural communities has already led to moves to lower the wolf's protected status and permit more culling. Whether Europe can share its crowded landscapes with a large predator may ultimately depend less on biology than on whether the people who bear the costs feel they are being heard.
